extracted.intended_audience: legislators, patent practitioners, USPTO stakeholders, and policy advocates involved in patent reform and USPTO funding
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements relating to USPTO funding mechanisms, annual planning and auditing, patent-term extension timing, and substantive patent-system reforms (e.g., first-inventor-to-file, reexamination). Meant to guide drafting, oversight, and evaluation of patent reform legislation and USPTO operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual Spending Plan notification (30-day requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Not later than 30 days after the beginning of each fiscal year, the Director shall notify the Committees on Appropriations of both Houses of Congress of the plan for the obligation and expenditure of the total amount of the funds for that fiscal year in accordance with section 605 of the Science, State, Justice, Commerce, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2006 (Public Law 109-108; 119 Stat. 2334).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan must be provided within 30 days of fiscal year start; serves as formal notice to appropriations committees to enable oversight and budgeting in accordance with cited statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents required in Annual Spending Plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Each plan shall summarize the operations of the Office for the current fiscal year, including financial details and staff levels with respect to major activities; and detail the operating plan of the Office, including specific expense and staff needs, for the current fiscal year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan must include: (A) summary of operations with financial details and staff levels for major activities, and (B) a detailed operating plan with specific expense and staff needs for the current fiscal year. This is intended to enable congressional oversight and transparency about PTO operations and resource needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual independent audit of financial statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Under Secretary shall, on an annual basis, provide for an independent audit of the financial statements of the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such audit shall be conducted in accordance with generally acceptable accounting procedures. The results of the most recent audit are to be included in reporting. Purpose: independent verification of PTO financial statements to support accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fund business-type budget submission requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fund shall prepare and submit each year to the President a business-type budget in a manner, and before a date, as the President prescribes by regulation for the budget program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annual budget must be prepared/submitted to the President per presidential regulations and timing. This aligns PTO/Fund budgeting with executive budget processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surcharge crediting to USPTO Public Enterprise Fund
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding section 11(i)(1)(B), amounts collected pursuant to the surcharge imposed under section 11(i)(1)(A) shall be credited to the United States Patent and Trademark Office Public Enterprise Fund.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surcharges collected under specified statutory provision are earmarked/credited directly to the USPTO Public Enterprise Fund to ensure those specific receipts are available to the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-term extension filing window (60-day rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent holders who wish to file an extension of their patent have a 60-day window to make the routine application. There is no ambiguity in this timeframe; a patent holder can file an extension application any time within the 60-day period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice note: do not wait until the last day. The legislative debate emphasizes that the rule is clear, late filings are rare (example cited: of 700 since 1984 only four were late), and that retroactive changes to relieve late filers are problematic. The 60-day deadline should be treated as strict absent compelling reason to change the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to retroactive changes that favor a single litigant
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing the rules to apply a new definition or to retroactively alter the 60-day period in ongoing litigation (in a manner that appears to benefit only one company) is deeply concerning and creates a precedent of changing rules to benefit a single company's litigating position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative guidance/anti-pattern: avoid retroactive statutory amendments that single out or disproportionately advantage one party; such measures can cost consumers and government and undermine confidence in the rule of law. Stakeholder letters (e.g., GPhA) urge striking such retroactive provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve Fund mechanism for excess fees (Patent Trademark Fee Reserve Fund)
rubrics_metrics.description: The House-created Patent and Trademark Fee Reserve Fund: fees collected by the USPTO in excess of the amount appropriated in a fiscal year are to be deposited into the Reserve Fund; fees in the Reserve Fund may only be used for the operations of the Patent and Trademark Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: ensure that user fees collected are available only for PTO services and activities in support of the fee-paying community, while keeping the PTO budget part of the annual appropriations process—preserving Congressional oversight (the 'power of the purse'). This is presented as a compromise alternative to a revolving fund.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolving Fund model and oversight tradeoff
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate-passed legislation would have taken the PTO out of the appropriations process by setting up a revolving fund that would have allowed the Office to set fees and collect and spend money without appropriations legislation and congressional oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy tradeoff: a revolving fund grants the PTO fee-setting and spending autonomy (predictable, direct funding) but reduces annual congressional appropriations oversight. The Reserve Fund model is advanced as preserving oversight while keeping fees available to the PTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraint of House Rule 21 on converting discretionary spending
rubrics_metrics.description: House Rule 21 prohibits converting discretionary spending into mandatory spending; the Coburn amendment's formulation apparently violates House Rule 21.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative drafting must account for chamber rules: certain funding mechanisms or language that effectively create mandatory spending may be barred under House procedural rules. This informs which financing constructs are permissible in the House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift to first-inventor-to-file (priority system reform)
rubrics_metrics.description: H.R. 1249 shifts the U.S. patent system from first-to-invent to a 'first-inventor-to-file' system to align the U.S. with the rest of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale provided: first-to-invent is ambiguous and costly; first-inventor-to-file creates greater certainty, reduces costs in disputes over priority, and is presented as not disadvantaging small firms while improving international compatibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improved re-examination procedures for low-quality patents
rubrics_metrics.description: H.R. 1249 strengthens re-examination procedures, allowing experts at the PTO to review low-quality business-method patents against the best prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective: improve patent quality by enabling the PTO to more effectively reexamine and invalidate low-quality patents using robust prior-art review mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle that user fees should fund PTO services (anti-fee-diversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fees collected for PTO services are user-funded (the office is entirely fee funded) and such fees should be used for Patent and Trademark Office activities; concern expressed that diverting fees is improper and undermines PTO operations and timeliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy principle: user fees ought to be spent on the services for which they were paid; mechanisms (Reserve Fund, statutory language, appropriations commitments) are advocated to prevent diversion of fees to unrelated government spending. Political rhetoric frames fee diversion as immoral or unjust.
